title: Orchestration Routing and On-call Ownership — Whiteboard Sketch
content:
Purpose:
Quick capture of a whiteboard session about who "owns" which slices of the control plane surface, how routing decisions get made across regions, and the on-call/hand-off expectations for outages or capacity events. This is intentionally informal — aim is to drive a clearer ownership table and a small set of routing/rollback rules we can bake into runbooks and the orchestrator policies.

Top-level constraints and assumptions:
- Single control-plane codebase with region-aware config. We do not want per-region forks of the orchestration logic.
- Gateways (edge) are stateless proxies; orchestration owns policy decisions and fallback.
- Runtime adapters (k8s adapters, on-prem agents, bare-metal connectors) are the boundary where infra-specific concerns live.
- SLOs: 99.95% API availability for hosted API routes; dedicated/private have higher isolation but same latency budgets.

Glossary (quick):
- API Gateway: public ingress (global LB + edge fleet) that authenticates, rate-limits, and forwards to orchestrator.
- Orchestrator: control plane service that decides routing targets, applies rollout policies, performs canaries, triggers fallbacks.
- Runtime Adapter: per-platform adapter that knows how to talk to a runtime (GKE pool, Dedicated GPU pool, Private on-prem agent).
- Fallback Tier: ordered list of compatible model variants/regions to route to when primary target unavailable.

Current pain points mentioned during session:
- Ambiguous ownership on cross-region fallback decisions — who sets the ordered fallback list?
- On-call playbooks contain both Gateway and Orchestrator steps; runbooks often duplicate checks and cause confusion.
- Runtime adapter errors surface as 502s with little semantic mapping (is it capacity, auth, or serialization?).
- Rollbacks currently manual for multi-region rollouts. Need a policy for automated fallback vs automated rollback.

Proposed ownership boundaries (working draft):
- API Gateway (edge routing, auth, basic validation): eng-platform-networking. Responsibilities: TLS, WAF, rate-limits, LB health filtering. On-call: network rotation (pager-level 1 for external connectivity issues).
- Orchestrator (policy, routing decisions, rollouts, canary gating): platform-engineering core. Responsibilities: routing graph, rollout engine, global fallback policy, canary metrics. On-call: platform-engineering primary; responsible for functional failures (incorrect fallbacks, rollout misbehavior).
- Runtime Adapters (k8s-adapter, dedicated-adapter, private-agent): infra-adapters team. Responsibilities: translation to runtime APIs, resource gating, adapter-level health, deployment hooks. On-call: infra-adapters for adapter-level failures; platform-engineering for client-facing regressions if adapter causes incorrect routing.
- Observability & Tracing: observability team (tooling/infra). Responsibilities: ensure traces propagate from gateway->orchestrator->adapter->runtime, token-level cost metrics, slow path alerts. On-call: support for query-level alert escalations.

Routing policy sketch (priority and decision points):
1) Local preference: prefer same-region runtime unless capacity/health issues detected.
2) Model variant compatibility: use semantic compatibility table (quantized ok? kv-cache homogeneous?) maintained by model-onboarding.
3) Tiered fallback: primary -> regional fallback pool -> cross-region compatible pool -> lower-cost batch-tier (with explicit latency degradation).
4) Safety thresholds: if error rate spikes > X% for 2m during canary, either throttle traffic back to previous stable or auto-fallback to next tier depending on traffic volume and SLO exposure.
5) Cost-aware routing: only used when requested (per-customer policy) or if automatic-cost-optimizations enabled and within error bounds.

Example operational flows (short):
- Primary runtime becomes unhealthy: adapter pushes health=false -> orchestrator receives health event -> orchestrator marks node pool unhealthy and recomputes routing graph -> traffic routed to regional fallback pool -> gateway updates LB target weights via control-plane API.
- Canary fails metric gate: orchestrator marks canary as failed -> rollout halted + traffic rolled back to previous model version -> operator receives alert with runbook link.

Ownership matrix (text table):
- API Gateway: eng-platform-networking; pager: net-rot; runbook: /runbooks/gateway-basic.md
- Orchestrator policy engine: platform-engineering; pager: platform-rot; runbook: /runbooks/orchestrator-fallback.md
- k8s runtime-adapter: infra-adapters; pager: adapters-rot; runbook: /runbooks/adapter-k8s.md
- Dedicated GPU adapter: infra-adapters; pager: adapters-rot
- Private on-prem agent: infra-adapters + solutions-eng (escalation path)

Escalation and hand-off rules (practical):
- If gateway shows global connectivity issues (packet loss to multiple regions), network on-call owns until outage localized. If orchestrator logic is suspected (incorrect failover ordering, cascading fallbacks), platform-engineering on-call owns.
- Adapter errors that are recoverable within 5 minutes should remain with adapter on-call. If adapter causes customer-facing SLO breach > 5 minutes, escalate to platform-engineering lead and open an incident.
- Cross-team handoff checklist (for incidents):
  - Timestamped decision log (who changed routing, why)
  - Snapshot of routing graph and weights (automatically collected by orchestrator)
  - Link to last deploys (gateway/orchestrator/adapters)
  - Triage notes and initial mitigation steps attempted

Sensible defaults for runbooks (to be turned into runnable scripts):
- Gather: trace id, request token id, route, model id, target runtime id
- Quick checks: adapter health, adapter logs (last 5m), orchestrator policy log for route decision, LB health for target nodes
- Next steps: if adapter shows OOMs or capacity, scale pool -> if scaling fails, failover to next tier; if orchestrator misrouted, rollback to prior policy version.

Observability additions proposed in this doc:
- Add explicit "fallback.reason" tag on traces when orchestrator triggers a fallback so we can query root cause across many requests.
- Adapter-level semantic error codes (CAPACITY, AUTH, SERIALIZATION, DEPLOYMENT) returned upstream to orchestrator and surfaced in 5xx metrics with labels.
- Per-customer routing policy audit log (who changed fallback order, when) for audit/compliance in Dedicated/Private.

Open questions (we did not resolve on board):
- Who authoritatively manages the region-fallback ordered list? (Options: model-onboarding, orchestrator policies, or customer overrides maintained in orchestration config).
- Auto-rollbacks: when should they be allowed vs only manual? What is the risk appetite?
- Is cost-aware routing enabled by default for small customers? (Probably not; opt-in via quota/toggles).
- How do we surface adapter semantic errors without leaking internal hostnames or sensitive identifiers in logs for Private deployments?

Immediate action items (owners):
- Platform-engineering: draft a short RFC for "fallback ownership" and a concrete schema for fallback lists (due 2025-03-07) — owner: Maya R. Singh.
- Infra-adapters: standardize semantic error codes and add a shim that maps internal adapter errors to the semantic codes (due 2025-03-14) — owner: Ibrahim Al-Kazemi.
- Observability: add fallback.reason tag and a dashboard for fallback frequency by model/region (POC by 2025-03-21) — owner: Lena Gómez.
- eng-platform-networking: confirm runbook split between gateway vs orchestrator (mini-review meeting 2025-02-28) — owner: Ethan Park.

Notes-to-self / scribbles: 
- Keep the orchestrator policy small and declarative: fallback lists + gating rules + cost overrides. Complex heuristics (ML-based routing) can be a later layer that consumes the same schema.
- Avoid allowing per-customer arbitrary cross-region overrides without SRE approval for Dedicated/Private.

- sketch: whiteboard photo: GDrive link (mock) -> https://drive.google.com/mock/whiteboard/board-238
- previous routing atlas (read for context) -> confluence:control-plane-routing-atlas
- incident playbook template -> /runbooks/incident-playbook-template.md

End of sketch.

(Will convert to a short RFC once consensus on fallback ownership emerges.)
